battle.title: The Trade-off Tightrope
battle.description: Weigh options out loud and defend your choice like a senior engineer.

questions.text: Which answer to "HashMap or sorted array for lookups?" shows the strongest trade-off thinking?
options: HashMap, because it is always better than an array
Sorted array, because arrays are simpler and simple is always best
Either one works, it does not really matter in practice
HashMap: O(1) lookup, more memory. Sorted array: compact, O(log n) search, slow inserts
questions.answer: HashMap: O(1) lookup, more memory. Sorted array: compact, O(log n) search, slow inserts
questions.explanation: A strong answer names what each option gains and costs. Declaring a winner with no reasoning ('always better') or refusing to choose shows no engineering judgment.

questions.text: You gave a brute force O(n^2) solution and the interviewer asks, "Can you do better?" What do you do?
options: Say no, this is the best possible, and stop
Name the bottleneck, propose a hash set, and state the time versus space trade-off
Silently erase everything and start over with no explanation
Apologise repeatedly and ask for a hint immediately
questions.answer: Name the bottleneck, propose a hash set, and state the time versus space trade-off
questions.explanation: Interviewers want to see you find the bottleneck and trade space for time deliberately. Giving up or going silent hides your reasoning, and asking for a hint with no attempt looks passive.

questions.text: The interviewer asks why you picked a linked list over an array for a queue. Your reason was weak. What is the best response?
options: Defend the choice more loudly so it sounds confident
Say the interviewer told you to use it
Switch immediately to anything the interviewer hints at without thinking
Re-evaluate openly, admit what the choice costs, and change it if the trade-offs favour the alternative
questions.answer: Re-evaluate openly, admit what the choice costs, and change it if the trade-offs favour the alternative
questions.explanation: Interviewers reward honest, evidence-based reasoning. Defending a weak choice out of ego is a red flag, and flipping with no analysis shows you never had a reason in the first place.

questions.text: Which statement best ties a trade-off to the requirements?
options: Since reads dominate and the data is small, I will favour fast lookups over memory savings
I picked it because it is what I used in my last project
This is the optimal one, everybody knows that
Memory is cheap, so I never need to consider it
questions.answer: Since reads dominate and the data is small, I will favour fast lookups over memory savings
questions.explanation: A trade-off is only meaningful relative to requirements such as read/write ratio and data size. Appeals to habit, authority or 'memory is cheap' skip the reasoning interviewers are looking for.

questions.text: Two designs are close: one is faster, one is simpler to maintain. The interviewer wants a decision. What do you say?
options: Pick the faster one with no mention of maintenance
Say both are fine and leave it to the interviewer
Recommend one based on the stated goals, name what you give up, and say what would make you change your mind
Pick the simpler one only because you are more comfortable with it
questions.answer: Recommend one based on the stated goals, name what you give up, and say what would make you change your mind
questions.explanation: Seniors commit to a recommendation while being explicit about the cost and the conditions that would flip it. Dodging the decision or choosing out of comfort shows weak ownership.
